output:
Short answer
- Aim for an LED task lamp that is dimmable, produces the right lumens for desk work, and is certified (ENERGY STAR or equivalent). From your catalog memory the only named product is the Harbor Task Lamp — it’s listed as adjustable and good for focused work, but I don’t have any catalog data showing it is an energy‑efficient LED model. That needs verification before you buy.

Why an LED task lamp
- LEDs give large energy savings for the same light output versus incandescent/halogen and long life (typical savings commonly cited are on the order of tens of percent to >70% depending on the baseline lamp). They also allow compact, integrated designs with dimming and better lumen-per-watt performance.
- For focused desk work, you also want good color rendering, a neutral color temperature, and glare control to maintain comfort and productivity.

What to look for (recommended spec targets and why)
- Light output (lumens): ~400–800 lm directed on task. This generally produces comfortable task illuminance for reading/desk work without excess.
  - Evidence: Illuminance targets for office task lighting are commonly in the 300–500 lux range for reading/writing; matching lumen output to desk size and fixture optics is how you reach that range.
- Efficacy: ≥80 lm/W (higher is better). This gives good energy efficiency per lumen.
  - Evidence: lm/W directly measures how much light you get per watt and is the best energy-efficiency metric for lighting.
- Color temperature (CCT): 3500–4000 K for neutral-white office lighting (avoid too warm or too cool unless you have a preference).
- Color rendering (CRI): ≥80; ≥90 if color-critical tasks are performed.
- Dimming: integrated dimming (and multiple brightness steps) improves comfort and saves energy in real use.
- Controls: consider occupancy/motion sensors, auto-off timers, or centralized scheduling for common areas to reduce run time.
- Warranty & rated lifetime: minimum 25,000 hours (preferably 50,000+), and a 3–5 year warranty for commercial use.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or DLC where applicable, and look for manufacturer test reports (LM-79, LM-80) or equivalent performance data.
  - Evidence: Certification programs and standardized test reports are how you verify manufacturer performance and energy claims.

Evidence available in your catalog memory
- Harbor Task Lamp: catalog notes it is adjustable and suitable for focused desk work. That supports its functional suitability but does not prove energy efficiency or LED performance.
  - Claim requiring verification: whether the Harbor Task Lamp is an LED model, its lumens, watts, lm/W, CCT, CRI, certifications, rated life, and warranty — the catalog entry in memory doesn’t include those specs.

Claims you should verify before purchase
- Power draw (watts) and lumen output — to calculate real energy use and lumens per watt.
- Certifications: ENERGY STAR or DLC listing if you require third‑party verification of efficiency.
- Measured test reports (LM‑79/LM‑80) or manufacturer data on lumen maintenance and lifetime.
- Dimmability compatibility (with desk dimmer systems or task controls you plan to use).
- Warranty and return policy for commercial use.

Practical next steps I can take for you
- If you want, I can:
  - Search your procurement catalog for ENERGY STAR or LED desk/task lamps and return a short list with the relevant spec fields (watts, lumens, CCT, CRI, lm/W, certifications, warranty).
  - Pull up the Harbor Task Lamp spec sheet (if available in catalog) and flag which performance numbers are missing and need vendor verification.
  - Recommend specific replacement models (commercial LED task lamps commonly used in offices) and show how they compare on energy, lumens, and price — and mark any claims that need verification.

Which of those would you like me to do next? If you want me to search the catalog now, tell me whether to include only ENERGY STAR/DLC certified products or to show all LED lamps.
